title: Greco-Bactrian Kingdom
capsule: The Greco-Bactrian Kingdom was a Hellenistic state in Central Asia, founded c. 255 BC when Diodotus I, satrap of Bactria, broke away from the Seleucid Empire during the disorder following Antiochus II's wars. Cut off from the Aegean world by the rise of Parthia c. 247 BC, it maintained a sophisticated Greek urban culture in Bactria (northern Afghanistan) and eventually expanded under Demetrius I (r. c. 200–180 BC) into Gandhara and northwestern India — the largest Hellenistic expansion in area. Internal succession conflicts fragmented the kingdom into rival branches in Bactria and India; the Bactrian core was overrun c. 135–130 BC by Yuezhi (Tocharian) nomads from the north, while the Indo-Greek successors persisted in the Punjab until the early 1st century AD.
attestation: Boundaries from Seshat Cliopatria (Bennett et al., Scientific Data 2025; CC BY 4.0), digitized from standard historical atlases at ~0.07° resolution. The Greco-Bactrian Kingdom's territory is partly attested by coin hoards, royal coin series, and a few surviving inscriptions (notably at Ai-Khanoum); precise boundaries — particularly the eastern and northern limits — are reconstructed from numismatic findspots and Chinese Han sources and are approximate.
